paper_title: Routing Policy Optimization for Online Diffusion Reinforcement Learning

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Reinforcement learning can align visual generators with reward signals beyond their pretraining objectives, but existing score-function methods typically introduce stochasticity by perturbing the reverse denoising trajectory, leading to costly rollout-based optimization. We instead ask whether stochastic exploration can be introduced inside the generator while preserving its original sampler. Routing Policy Optimization (RPO) answers this question by turning attention routing into a stochastic exploration action. At a few selected denoising levels, each query block keeps its own block and samples further key blocks in proportion to the generator's native attention mass, or keeps dense attention. The sampled route perturbs the velocity of that transition, and a Gaussian likelihood around the dense velocity scores the perturbation with a score-function objective. RPO further uses a controlled two-rollout estimator: two rollouts share the same prompt, initial latent, routed denoising levels, and dense anchor layers, differing only in their sampled attention routes. Their reward difference provides an advantage signal for the routed transitions. Because the likelihood differentiates the dense velocity itself, the learned updates remain effective after routing is removed. At inference, RPO restores dense attention and retains the original deterministic sampler. Experiments on text-to-image and text-to-video generation show that RPO improves generation quality while achieving nearly 4x higher training efficiency than Flow-GRPO-style methods. Please see our project page at https://velox-world.com/rpo for visual results.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Diffusion and flow models now generate high-quality images and videos from natural-language prompts (Shen et al., 2026b; Li & Wang, 2026). DDPM establishes stochastic reverse denoising, while DDIM exposes deterministic sampling path under the same training objective (Ho et al., 2020; Song et al., 2021). Flow matching and rectified flow instead learn vector fields for continuous transport (Lipman et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023; Esser et al., 2024). In parallel, latent diffusion, Diffusion Transformers, and video diffusion models make high-resolution visual generation tractable at scale (Rombach et al., 2021; Peebles & Xie, 2022; Yang et al., 2024; Wan Team et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2026). Learned preference models then expose alignment objectives beyond likelihood and reconstruction (Xu et al., 2023; Kirstain et al., 2023; Ma et al., 2025). Online reinforcement learning can optimize these objectives, but its central bottleneck is the policy. DDPO and DPOK treat stochastic denoising transitions as actions (Black et al., 2024; Fan et al., 2023). Flow-GRPO and DanceGRPO extend this construction to deterministic flow models by converting their ODE samplers into stochastic SDEs (Liu et al., 2025a; Xue et al., 2025b). Temporal windows, shared branches, and one-step updates reduce the resulting rollout cost (Li et al., 2025a; He et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025b; He et al., 2026), while dense credit and regulated clipping improve how terminal rewards shape sampler transitions (Deng et al., 2026; Shen et al., 2026a; Yang et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2025a). Forward-matching objectives avoid reverse-trajectory likelihoods, but they also remove the explicit sampled action (Zheng et al., 2026; Luo et al., 2026; Xue et al., 2025a; Xu et al., 2026c; Choi et al., 2026). What remains missing is an explicit, tractable policy that preserves the original deterministic sampler for both image and video generators. Corresponding author.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: Figure 1: controlled routing pair replaces large sampler-noise group. Sampler-space GRPO injects continuous noise into the reverse process and estimates an advantage from many complete visual rollouts. RPO retains the original deterministic sampler and pairs two rollouts that share the prompt, initial visual latent, routed denoising levels, and anchor layers. They differ only in their sampled attention routes, so their reward difference measures the aggregate effect of the two recorded routed trajectories. Generated visual outputs are schematic. Our key insight is that stochastic exploration need not perturb the denoising trajectory. diffusion transformer splits each latent into visual tokens, and its attention layers already decide how much each token attends to the others. If we group neighboring tokens into blocks, each query block can attend to sampled subset of key blocks instead of all of them as dense attention does. We call this choice of visible key blocks route. Sampling routes exposes stochastic action without adding policy head or modifying the sampler. We introduce Routing Policy Optimization (RPO), which samples attention routes from the generators own attention mass at few denoising levels. Each sampled route perturbs the velocity of its transition, and Gaussian likelihood around the dense velocity scores this perturbation. This likelihood supplies score-function surrogate for the dense generator itself. The routing action also enables controlled two-rollout estimator, as Figure 1 illustrates. Both members share every non-routing source of variation and differ only in their sampled routes. Their signed reward difference therefore provides leave-one-out advantage for the two routed trajectories. During replay, each routed transition is scored from its recorded input, so later levels condition on earlier routes. Routing serves only as training interface. The pass that proposes routes carries no gradient, and the likelihood differentiates the dense velocity. The update therefore acts on the same velocity field that dense inference evaluates. After training, we remove all masks and evaluate the updated generator with dense attention and its original deterministic sampler. The central empirical question is whether reward learned through temporary routing transfers to the dense image or video generator used at inference. We evaluate this question on Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium and Wan2.2-TI2V-5B (Wan Team et al., 2025), covering text-to-image and text-to-video generation. Across both settings, RPO improves reward-aligned generation quality while retaining dense inference. On Stable Diffusion 3.5, RPO exceeds the final dense validation reward of Flow-GRPO within 25 of 50 training steps and ends 1.1 points higher. On Wan2.2, RPO attains the strongest overall VBench score among the evaluated checkpoints while using 24.1 GPU-hours, compared with 75.4 for Flow-GRPO and 102.3 for DanceGRPO. This corresponds to 3.1 and 4.2 lower training cost, respectively. Our contributions can be summarized as following: We introduce sampler-preserving formulation for online alignment of continuous visual generators. Its exploration action is training-time attention route sampled from native attention mass, with no auxiliary policy head or SDE conversion.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: We score each routed transition with Gaussian velocity likelihood around the dense velocity and optimize it with controlled two-rollout surrogate that holds the non-routing generation context fixed. Because this likelihood updates the dense velocity directly, we remove routing at inference and preserve the original image or video sampler. We validate RPO on Stable Diffusion 3.5 and Wan2.2, demonstrating improved reward-aligned quality across image and video generation together with substantially lower training cost than sampler-space baselines.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Reward alignment methods for visual generators differ mainly in where the learning signal enters the generator. We organize prior work along this axis, from the sampler trajectory to the attention computation. Sampler-space policy gradients. DDPO and DPOK first treated stochastic denoising transitions as policy actions (Black et al., 2024; Fan et al., 2023). Flow-GRPO and DanceGRPO carried this view to flow matching and video by converting the deterministic sampler into an SDE and estimating group-relative advantages (Liu et al., 2025a; Xue et al., 2025b). Follow-up work lowers the cost of these stochastic trajectories. Temporal windows, shared-prefix branches, and one-step updates reduce the number or cost of stochastic transitions (Li et al., 2025a;b; He et al., 2026). TempFlow-GRPO concentrates stochasticity at designated branch points for temporal credit assignment (He et al., 2025), and TAGRPO aligns trajectories that start from identical initial noise (Wang et al., 2026). Dense temporal and spatial credit or regulated clipping further improve how terminal reward shapes each transition (Deng et al., 2026; Shen et al., 2026a; Yang et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2025a). These methods keep the action inside the sampler, so exploration still perturbs the reverse trajectory. Objectives without sampler actions. second family avoids sampler actions. Direct reward finetuning backpropagates through differentiable image or video rewards (Clark et al., 2023; Prabhudesai et al., 2024). For black-box rewards, DiffusionNFT, DGPO, and advantage-weighted matching replace reverse-trajectory likelihoods with forward-process or preference objectives (Zheng et al., 2026; Luo et al., 2026; Xue et al., 2025a). Adjoint matching, ELBO surrogates, path-space value gradients, and velocity matching pursue the same goal through native regression targets (Bergmeister et al., 2026; Tang et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026c; Choi et al., 2026). For few-step generators, hybrid scheme combines distribution matching, GRPO on stochastic intermediate transitions, and reward backpropagation through the final step (Huang et al., 2026). Offline preference optimization removes online rollouts altogether, ranging from Diffusion-DPO to multidimensional and temporally dense video preferences (Wallace et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024; 2025b; Wu et al., 2025b). These objectives leave inference untouched, but they give up an explicit sampled action. In contrast, RPO keeps score-function policy with recorded action and places that action inside attention. Discrete actions and attention routing. Discrete policies already exist in visual generation. MaskGRPO, Mask-GRPO, and MaskFocus optimize token corruption, unmasking, or mask schedules in natively discrete image generators (Ma et al., 2026; Luo et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025a). Structured attention sparsity is also well studied, although mainly for efficiency. Q/K-derived block gates and training-free compression expose attention redundancy (Gao et al., 2024; Yuan et al., 2024; Xi et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025). VSA, trainable dynamic routing, and hierarchical sparse attention learn such sparsity inside image and video generators (Zhang et al., 2025b; Zhao et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2025; Lv et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026a). Reinforcement learning has also selected sparse-attention levels or recomputation schedules for acceleration (Zhao et al., 2026; Aliev et al., 2026). KVPO comes closest to alignment. It explores through stochastic historical-key routing in autoregressive video and scores branches with velocity-energy surrogate (Zhang et al., 2026). Other work optimizes attention allocation for multimodal reasoning or routes preference credit through diffusion attention (Li et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026b). Dropout-GRPO samples Bernoulli masks to diversify deterministic latent reasoning (Jung, 2026). Our paired estimator also builds on common random numbers and group-relative baselines (Asmussen & Glynn, 2007; Shao et al., 2024), and 2-GRPO shows that two language-model rollouts can retain most of larger groups performance (Wu

sections.title: 4 ROUTING POLICY OPTIMIZATION
sections.content: Sampler-space methods explore by injecting noise into the reverse trajectory. RPO instead explores by routing attention at the routed levels. We first define how the generators own attention proposes routes (Section 4.1), then score each routed transition with Gaussian likelihood around the dense velocity (Section 4.2), and finally turn the reward difference of matched pair into policy-gradient update (Section 4.3). Figure 2 summarizes this path.

sections.title: 5 EXPERIMENTS
sections.content: Our experiments test whether reward learned through temporary routing transfers to the dense generator used at inference. After the setup, we evaluate text-to-image generation (Section 5.2), compare learning speed with sampler-space RL (Section 5.3), and measure VBench transfer and training cost on video (Section 5.4). 5.1 SETUP Image setting. We train Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium (Esser et al., 2024) on prompts from the PickScore SFW split (Kirstain et al., 2023). Each rollout generates 512 512 image with deterministic 10-step flow sampler and no classifier-free guidance. The training reward is HPSv3 (Ma et al., 2025) scaled by 0.1. After training, we evaluate the dense model on DrawBench prompts (Saharia et al., 2022). An aesthetic score and DeQA-Score (You et al., 2025) measure image quality, while ImageReward (Xu et al., 2023), PickScore, and UnifiedReward (Wang et al., 2025b) measure preference. During training, we evaluate the dense model every 5 steps on 64 fixed validation prompts with 28-step sampler. Video setting. We train Wan2.2-TI2V-5B (Wan Team et al., 2025), text-to-video flow-matching generator, on curated creative prompt distribution. Each rollout renders 13 frames at 704 1280 with 10-step sampler and classifier-free guidance scale 5. The reward is HPSv3 scaled by 0.1 and is computed on every fourth frame. Baselines and training. On SD3.5, we compare against Flow-GRPO (Liu et al., 2025a). It trains the same LoRA adapters with the same HPSv3 reward and the same 10-step training sampler, but it explores by sampling SDE trajectories. On Wan2.2, we compare against Flow-GRPO and DanceGRPO (Xue et al., 2025b). Both baselines train the same generator with the same HPSv3 reward and also explore through SDE trajectories. DanceGRPO uses groups of = 8 and updates the full model. On both generators, RPO instead collects 64 matched pairs (G = 2) per training step. Appendix lists the routing and optimization settings for both generators. Appendix details the evaluation protocols. 5.2 TEXT-TO-IMAGE GENERATION Figure 3 first compares SD3.5 Medium before and after RPO training on DrawBench. RPO improves all five metrics, although none of them is the training reward. The preference metrics show the

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: (a) HPSv3 reward on each methods training rollouts. Figure 4: RPO learns faster than Flow-GRPO on Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium. Both methods train the same LoRA adapters with HPSv3 reward and 10-step training sampler for 50 steps from the same base model. (a) Mean raw HPSv3 of each steps training rollouts (faint) and its exponential moving average with smoothing weight 0.6 (bold). (b) Raw HPSv3 of the dense model on 64 fixed validation prompts with 28-step sampler, measured every 5 steps from step 0. (b) HPSv3 reward of the dense model on validation prompts. clearest gains. ImageReward rises from 0.54 to 0.18, and UnifiedReward rises from 2.10 to 2.32. Image quality also improves, with DeQA-Score rising from 3.35 to 3.56. In the samples, the trained model writes the requested storefront text and renders clear brown giraffe, whereas the base model misses both. Because each pair shares its prompt, initial noise, and sampler, these gains come from the updated weights of the dense generator alone. 5.3 LEARNING SPEED AGAINST SAMPLER-SPACE RL Online RL pays for every rollout, so the reward gained per training step matters as much as the final score. Figure 4 tracks RPO and Flow-GRPO over 50 training steps on SD3.5 Medium. Both runs start from the same base model, which scores 3.94 and 3.96 on their shared validation. Figure 4a reports the reward of the rollouts that each method samples during training. The smoothed RPO reward rises above 9 by step 30 and stays near 9.5, whereas the smoothed Flow-GRPO reward stays below 8. However, RPO scores routed rollouts and Flow-GRPO scores SDE rollouts, so neither curve measures the dense model used at inference. Figure 4b therefore reports the decisive comparison on the dense model. Flow-GRPO starts slightly faster at step 5, but RPO leads from step 10 onward. RPO reaches 8.90 at step 25, which already exceeds the step-50 score of Flow-GRPO, 8.81. It peaks at 10.20 at step 40 and ends at 9.91. Over the full run, RPO gains +5.97 over its step-zero score, whereas Flow-GRPO gains +4.86. RPO thus matches the final dense reward of Flow-GRPO in half the training steps and ends 1.1 points higher. Both curves come from one training seed, and Appendix lists the remaining differences between the two runs. Exploration through attention routing therefore turns each training step into more dense-model reward than exploration through SDE trajectories. 5.4 VBENCH TRANSFER AND TRAINING COST single reward scalar compresses appearance and semantics, so reward gains alone do not establish broad video quality. We therefore evaluate the base model and the three trained checkpoints on VBench, which decomposes video generation into 16 fine-grained dimensions with tailored prompts and evaluation procedures (Huang et al., 2024). Each model generates 6,220 13-frame videos from shared prompts and initial noise with deterministic sampler (Appendix D). Table 1 lists the 8 dimensions where RPO exceeds both RL baselines, together with the overall score and training cost. The largest gains over the base model are semantic. Object class improves by +4.40, human action by +4.80, scene by +3.43, and multiple objects by +2.15. RPO also improves aesthetic quality, imaging quality, subject consistency, and motion smoothness over the base model. It is the only trained checkpoint above the base model overall. Moreover, it trains with 24.1 GPU-hours, which is 3.1 less than Flow-GRPO and 4.2 less than DanceGRPO, although the runs are not compute-matched.

RPO follows the prompt more closely and replaces distorted, painterly textures with coherent, realistic scenes. The remaining dimensions reveal trade-offs. RPO lowers color and appearance style relative to the base model, although it still leads the trained baselines on color. Flow-GRPO raises dynamic degree by 12.50 points but loses consistency, smoothness, aesthetic quality, color, and object-class accuracy. RPO therefore transfers reward mainly through semantic alignment, whereas Flow-GRPO trades visual quality for motion. The four Wan2.2 overall scores span only 0.81 points on one seed set, so we read the aggregate ranking as directional. CogVideoX-5B (Yang et al., 2024) and HunyuanVideo (Kong et al., 2024) serve as external references under matched prompts and scoring. Figure 5 makes these semantic gains visible on four held-out prompts, where the RPO videos follow the prompts more closely. Both checkpoints run dense attention with the same prompt, initial noise, and sampler, so they differ only in their weights. Across image and video, the gains learned through routing persist after the masks are removed.

sections.title: 6 DISCUSSION AND LIMITATIONS
sections.content: RPO places its policy action inside attention, and this design choice also defines its current limits. First, the framework is confined to attention. Its action is mask over key-value blocks, so it requires backbone that computes attention. We have not yet generalized routing to other architectures, where no attention mass exists to propose routes. Second, the routing proposal and its likelihood are coarse. Each route logit averages the attention mass of whole block over every routed layer and head, which hides token-level and layer-specific structure. Moreover, the velocity likelihood treats the routed deviation as Gaussian, although discrete route produces it. finer proposal and likelihood that also credits the route choice could give the policy more faithful view of which blocks matter. Finally, RPO currently adapts to an existing generator rather than shaping it. Co-designing the network architecture with RPO is promising direction for achieving both higher efficiency and larger RL gains.

sections.title: 7 CONCLUSION
sections.content: In this work, we addressed the cost of online reinforcement learning for visual generators without perturbing their reverse denoising trajectories. We introduced Routing Policy Optimization, samplerpreserving method that samples block-wise attention routes from the generators native attention mass at few selected denoising levels. controlled pair holds the non-routing generation context fixed, so its reward difference weights Gaussian velocity likelihood of the two recorded routed trajectories. Because this likelihood updates the dense velocity field, inference removes the masks and restores dense attention under the original deterministic sampler. Experiments on Stable Diffusion 3.5 and Wan2.2 demonstrate improved reward-aligned quality across text-to-image and text-to-video generation while requiring substantially less training compute than sampler-space baselines. By moving stochastic exploration from the sampler into attention, RPO provides an efficient policy interface for reward-aligned visual generation without altering the inference process.

sections.title: A GILBERT BLOCKS AND THE SAFETY SET
sections.content: Section 3 places every routing decision on block of visual tokens and protects safety set Sq. This appendix gives the full construction that both generators use. We first explain why the token order matters and define the frame-sliced Gilbert order. We then define the blocks, the safety set, and the executed attention mask, and we report the resulting block and candidate counts for Wan2.2 and Stable Diffusion 3.5. Why the token order matters. routing unit covers contiguous run of tokens, and one draw keeps or drops whole run as key block. Both generators store visual tokens in raster order, which scans each latent frame row by row. contiguous raster run is therefore thin horizontal strip. On the 32 32 token grid of Stable Diffusion 3.5, 128-token run spans four entire image rows. Its attention mass mixes tokens that lie far apart, while its vertical neighbors lie whole rows away in the sequence. As result, route decision on raster run couples unrelated content, and small spatial neighborhood cannot be expressed as few runs. The token order should instead turn every contiguous run into compact spatial patch.

A.1 FRAME-SLICED GILBERT ORDER generalized Hilbert curve, or Gilbert curve, visits every cell of rectangle of arbitrary size exactly once and moves to an adjacent cell at every step. Jenga (Zhang et al., 2025c) partitions video tokens along such curve for block-sparse attention, and we adopt the frame-sliced variant of its released implementation. Let the visual latent contain frames of tokens, so it holds = HW tokens. Token = (f, m, n) lies in frame {0, . . . , 1}, row m, and column n. The order assigns each token rank: γ(f, m, n) = HW + gH,W (ϕf (m, n)) . (9) Here gH,W assigns the ranks 1, . . . , HW along the two-dimensional Gilbert curve of an grid, which starts and ends at the two corners of one longer side. The map ϕf reflects the rows, the columns, or both, so that frame starts at the corner nearest to the end of frame 1. The first map ϕ0 is the identity, and the offset HW keeps every frame contiguous. Intuitively, the curve fills one frame, steps to the same spatial position in the next frame, and fills that frame in reflected direction. Every step therefore moves to neighboring token, including the step across frame boundary. Figure 6 contrasts this order with the raster order. Contiguous runs of this order are compact patches. Bidirectional attention. Both generators denoise all visual tokens jointly with bidirectional selfattention, so every query can attend to every frame. The order therefore depends only on the latent grid and not on generation schedule. We compute it once per resolution and reuse it for all routed layers, heads, noise levels, and rollouts. Reordering inside attention. The order acts only inside each routed self-attention layer. After the native projections, query-key normalization, and rotary position embedding where the generator uses one, we permute the queries, keys, and values into Gilbert order. We then apply the routed mask and permute the output back to raster order. Dense attention is equivariant to shared permutation of its queries, keys, and values, and every positional signal is attached before the permutation. The reordering thus changes which token pairs share routing decision, but it leaves positions and the dense computation unchanged. At inference, RPO runs the stock dense attention without any reordering. Intuitively, the route decides which non-local context each query block sees, while its own patch always stays visible. Text conditioning. Routing acts only on visual self-attention. sections.title: B IMPLEMENTATION DETAILS
sections.content: This appendix lists the settings behind Section 5.1. The routing proposal and objective are identical for both generators. Only the routing hyperparameters, the rollout step, and the optimization settings differ. Stable Diffusion 3.5. The reference configuration routes levels 2, 3, and 4 of the 10-step training sampler with level weights wt of 1, 0.76, and 0.5 and temperature = 1. Each 128-token query block keeps its own block and one candidate, or attends densely (κ = 1/32, Ku = 1). One draw per query block serves all 24 joint-attention layers and the 13 image-only self-attention layers, and 16 of the 24 transformer blocks act as anchor layers at each routed level. Rollouts use the centered routed step. At routed level, the rollout draws second, unrecorded route and steps with vθ(xt, t, c) + (vt,(1) vt,(2))/2, where vt,(1) and vt,(2) are the velocities under the two routes. The perturbation then has zero mean, so the rollout stays close to the dense path, and the likelihood of Equation 4 applies unchanged to the recovered velocity. Each wave contains 64 prompt groups at = 2, split into two optimizer minibatches of 32 groups. We train rank-32 LoRA adapters with 4, and no α = 64 on the eight attention projections, with learning rate 1.4 10 warmup. Advantage processing uses 5% winsorization and batch-IQR scaling with floor 0.03, and no pair is gated. sections.title: D EVALUATION PROTOCOLS
sections.content: Comparison with DanceGRPO. The DanceGRPO run uses the same generator and reward as RPO. Three differences remain. First, DanceGRPO is full-model GRPO with = 8 and stochastic SDE sampler, whereas RPO routes two denoising transitions with = 2. Second, the two runs use different rollout backends. Third, the DanceGRPO run follows longer 120-step schedule. VBench. We evaluate all 16 VBench dimensions on the standard prompt suite. Each Wan2.2 model generates 6,220 videos with 13 frames at 704 1280 and 24 fps, using deterministic 50-step ODE sampler with classifier-free guidance scale 5.0. The four Wan2.2 models share prompts and initial noise. CogVideoX-5B and HunyuanVideo use the same prompts, frame count, denoising steps, and scoring, but they keep their native resolution and guidance. Their rows therefore provide reference under matched content and scoring, although their generation settings and training compute differ. Training GPU-hours use common accounting scope and exclude VBench evaluation. Stable Diffusion 3.5. During training, dense evaluation uses 28-step sampler and reports raw HPSv3 on 64 held-out prompts. Early runs draw this subset with the training seed. For controlled seed comparisons, we instead use fixed 64-prompt file and fixed validation noise seed. The DrawBench evaluation in Figure 3 uses 1,000 images from 200 prompts and 5 seeds, generated without classifier-free guidance. Comparison with Flow-GRPO on Stable Diffusion 3.5. The two runs in Figure 4 share the validation protocol, namely the fixed 64-prompt file, 28-step dense sampler with guidance scale 1.0, fixed noise seed, and raw HPSv3. Their step-zero scores are 3.941 for RPO and 3.955 for Flow-GRPO. Both runs train rank-32 LoRA adapters with α = 64 on the same attention projections, use 10-step training sampler with guidance scale 1.0 at 512 512, and use training seed 42. However, the two runs collect rollouts with different backends. On the base weights and the same 10-step dense sampler, the RPO backend scores 0.92 raw HPSv3, whereas the Flow-GRPO backend scores 1.38. The training rewards in Figure 4a therefore mix method and backend effects, and the dense validation in Figure 4b is the controlled comparison.

sections.title: E EXTENDED DISCUSSION
sections.content: Known failure modes. Two failure modes remain open. The first is dense-gain fade. In some runs, the dense-inference gain peaks and then decays, while the reward of the routed training rollouts

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: keeps rising. The generator then improves its routed transitions faster than its dense ones. Centered routed steps keep the rollouts near the dense path and reduce this split on Stable Diffusion 3.5, but the mechanism is not fully isolated. The second is reward hacking against the frozen preference model. This risk is general to online RL for generative models and is not specific to RPO. Both failure modes suggest that scalar terminal reward is coarse supervisor for routed exploration action. Estimator scope. The velocity likelihood in Equation 5 is surrogate rather than the exact likelihood of the sampled route. It models the routed deviation as an isotropic Gaussian around the dense velocity, whereas the true deviation is the effect of discrete route on the attention output. It also omits the pathwise gradient of the generator through later denoising transitions and through the frozen reward model. Finally, the width s2 is re-estimated on every batch. As routing perturbs the generator less during training, s2 shrinks, so the same deviation produces larger gradient. Extensions. Two directions extend the method naturally. likelihood that adds the probability of the sampled route to the velocity term would also credit the route choice itself, rather than only its effect on the dense velocity. Larger groups would give leave-one-out baseline with more members. They trade part of the pairs variance cancellation for more stable advantage scale. Both extensions are compatible with the estimator as stated.
